messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: type punning & aliasing warning
parts:
On 6/30/12 5:15 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I'm fine on g++ 4.4 now. Although I do see this warning message in several places now
>
> src/stan/agrad/partials_vari.hpp:95: warning: dereferencing type-punned pointer will break strict-aliasing rules
>
> which I thoroughly understand up through "dereferencing".

Quick question on builds: did we set a no-aliasing flag
or is it on by default? It's more dangerous, but may help
with performance.

Here's the theory:

"Type punning" means converting non-interoperable types.

"Aliasing" means using two differently named pointers to
the same memory.

With a "no-aliasing" option, we're telling the compiler
that we promise not to change the values of an array it's working
on from the outside using an alias. That lets the compiler
know it can look up values in parallel without fear of them
being changed out from under it.

Here's our code; line 95, where the warning occurs, is marked.

template <typename T1, typename T2, typename T3>
class partials3_vari : public vari {
private:
const static size_t nvars_ = !stan::is_constant<T1>::value +
!stan::is_constant<T2>::value +
!stan::is_constant<T3>::value;
vari* operands_[nvars_];
double partials_[nvars_];

public:
partials3_vari(double value,
T1 operand1, double partial1,
T2 operand2, double partial2,
T3 operand3, double partial3)
: vari(value) {
size_t i = 0;
if (!stan::is_constant<T1>::value) {
operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand1);
partials_[i] = partial1;
i++;
}
if (!stan::is_constant<T2>::value) {
**95** operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand2);
partials_[i] = partial2;
i++;
}
if (!stan::is_constant<T3>::value) {
operands_[i] = *(vari**)(&operand3);
partials_[i] = partial3;
}
}

When T2 is double, a type pun is created by line 95.
It's trying to cast a reference to double into
a reference to a vari**, which will cause undefined
behavior. BUT, we never actually face such a cast,
because if T2 is double, the trait condition
stan::is_constant<T2>::value is true and thus the
if condition is false. In fact, with optimization,
the instructions should just disappear because the
loop condition can be evaluated statically.

- Bob
